subject: feminism
title: Fourth Wave (c. 2010s–): when the machine was the hashtag
dek: A Toronto police officer comment, a British website for everyday stories, Tarana Burke phrase from 2006, and two 2017 investigations made hashtag feminism look global and instant. The wave number came after. The activism was not one platform.

thumb.alt: Aerial view of massive crowd at Women March on Washington, January 21, 2017.

hero.alt: Wide photograph of the Women March on Washington filling streets near the Capitol, January 21, 2017. Massive crowds stretch into the distance, many wearing pink hats, holding signs.
hero.caption: The Women March on Washington, 21 January 2017, the day after Donald Trump inauguration. An estimated 500,000 people gathered in Washington, with millions more in sister marches worldwide. This is a demonstration of scale, not a picture of the hashtag that would follow in October. The march is its own fact: women and allies in the streets, visible and counted.
hero.credit: Rosa Pineda / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

honesty: Fourth wave is a later Anglo-American journalistic and classroom name, not what most participants called themselves in 2012 or 2017. The machine that changed was digital: smartphones, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, later TikTok. Dates are conveniences: Toronto SlutWalk in 2011, the Everyday Sexism Project in 2012, Burke Me Too from 2006, the 2017 Weinstein reporting, Women March in January 2017. Many contemporary photographs are still in copyright or require model releases. The images here are free-licensed or public-domain: a 2017 march, a 2011 SlutWalk. Where a usable photograph could not be found, the lesson names the event without a picture.

timeline.label: SlutWalk
timeline.detail: 3 April 2011: first SlutWalk in Toronto after Toronto Police Constable Michael Sanguinetti told York University students at a 24 January safety talk that women should avoid dressing like sluts to prevent victimization. Sonya Barnett and Heather Jarvis organized.

timeline.label: Everyday Sexism / Delhi
timeline.detail: 16 April 2012: Laura Bates launched the Everyday Sexism Project in the UK. 16 December 2012: gang rape and murder of Jyoti Singh on a Delhi bus sparked massive protests across India.

timeline.label: Ni Una Menos
timeline.detail: 3 June 2015: mass protests across Argentina after the murder of 14-year-old Chiara Páez. Over 200,000 gathered in Buenos Aires. Not One Woman Less.

timeline.label: Black Protest
timeline.detail: 3 October 2016: Czarny Protest, Poland Black Monday. Tens of thousands struck from work and school to oppose a proposed total abortion ban. Parliament rejected the bill days later.

timeline.label: Women March / Weinstein / MeToo
timeline.detail: 21 January 2017: Women March. 5 October 2017: Jodi Kantor and Megan Twohey in the New York Times. 10 October: Ronan Farrow in The New Yorker. 15 October: Alyssa Milano tweet. Burke Me Too, from 2006, became a cascade.

timeline.label: Time's Up / tal-corset
timeline.detail: 1 January 2018: Time's Up Legal Defense Fund launched. South Korea Escape the Corset movement around 2018.

fun_fact.title: Alyssa Milano 15 October 2017 tweet was not the origin of Me Too
fun_fact.text: When actress Alyssa Milano tweeted on 15 October 2017 asking people to reply if they had been harassed, she did not know that activist Tarana Burke had been using the phrase since 2006 for community work with survivors. Within days, Black women on social media credited Burke as the founder. Milano acknowledged this. Burke had created Just Be Inc. in 2003 in Selma, Alabama. The hashtag in 2017 made the phrase global and instant. The movement is a decade older.

glossary.explain: A later journalistic and classroom label for feminist work from roughly the early 2010s onward. The machine that changed was digital infrastructure: smartphones, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok. SlutWalk, Everyday Sexism, Delhi 2012, Ni Una Menos, MeToo. Most people in the work did not call it a wave.

Protests beginning 3 April 2011 in Toronto after Toronto Police Constable Michael Sanguinetti told York University students that women should avoid dressing like sluts. Organized by Sonya Barnett and Heather Jarvis. A march against victim-blaming and rape culture.

American activist, born 1973. Founded Just Be Inc. in 2003 in Selma, Alabama, for young women of color. Began using the phrase Me Too in 2006 in community work with survivors of sexual violence. The 2017 hashtag MeToo spread her phrase globally, but the movement is hers from 2006.

Phrase coined by Tarana Burke in 2006 for empathy-based healing with survivors of sexual violence, especially Black girls and women. Became a viral hashtag in October 2017 after Alyssa Milano tweet following the Weinstein reporting.

American film producer. Allegations of sexual harassment, assault, and rape against him, spanning decades, were reported in October 2017 by Kantor/Twohey and Farrow. Convicted of rape in New York 2020. The public accusations against him catalyzed the MeToo cascade.
New York Times investigative reporter. With Megan Twohey, published the 5 October 2017 Harvey Weinstein investigation. Pulitzer Prize for Public Service, 2018.
New York Times investigative reporter. With Jodi Kantor, published the 5 October 2017 Harvey Weinstein investigation. Pulitzer Prize for Public Service, 2018.
Investigative journalist. Published Harvey Weinstein investigation in The New Yorker on 10 October 2017. NBC News passed on the story. Pulitzer Prize for Public Service, 2018.

Mass protest on 21 January 2017, the day after Donald Trump inauguration. An estimated 500,000 in Washington, D.C., with millions in over 600 sister marches worldwide. At the time, the largest single-day demonstration in U.S. history.
Argentine feminist movement born 3 June 2015 after the murder of 14-year-old Chiara Páez. Mass protests across 70 Argentine cities. Not One Woman Less. Opposes femicide and gender violence.
Website launched by Laura Bates on 16 April 2012 in the UK for people to document experiences of daily sexism. Over 100,000 entries by 2015. Branches in 25 countries.

Initiative launched 1 January 2018 by Hollywood women. The Time's Up Legal Defense Fund, housed at the National Women's Law Center, provides legal and media support to survivors. Raised over 22 million by end of 2018.

sections.title: The machine the third wave used, and what a different machine could do

blocks.text: The Third Wave lesson in this archive ends in the early 2010s, when third wave was already a heading in a syllabus. That lesson notes that hashtag campaigns used a different machine from a photocopied zine, a C-SPAN weekend, or a UN platform. This lesson is about that different machine. It is a description of how digital infrastructure—smartphones, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram, later TikTok—changed what feminism could look like in public, what speed meant, what a crowd was, and who could call one.

By 2010 the machine had changed. Facebook had 608 million users. Twitter had 54 million. Smartphones put both platforms in people pockets. A photograph taken at a protest in one city could be in another city feed before the march ended. A phrase like Me Too, which Tarana Burke had been using since 2006 in community work in Selma, Alabama, could become a global hashtag in October 2017 in the hours after an actress tweeted it. The speed was new. The platform was new. The problem—men using power to assault and silence women—was not.

sections.title: A police officer, a website, a bus, two investigations, and a march

blocks.text: On 24 January 2011 Toronto Police Constable Michael Sanguinetti spoke at a York University campus safety forum. Sanguinetti said, according to reports, women should avoid dressing like sluts in order not to be victimized. The comment was reported in the university newspaper. Heather Jarvis and Sonya Barnett organized a march for 3 April 2011. They called it SlutWalk. Three thousand people showed up in Toronto. Within months, sister walks took place in cities worldwide.

blocks.alt: Photograph of the first SlutWalk protest in Toronto, 3 April 2011. Crowd of protesters on a city street.
blocks.caption: The first SlutWalk in Toronto, 3 April 2011, organized by Sonya Barnett and Heather Jarvis after Constable Michael Sanguinetti January comment. The march reclaimed the word slut and protested victim-blaming. Sister walks followed in cities worldwide.
blocks.credit: Anton Bielousov / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 3.0

blocks.text: On 16 April 2012 Laura Bates, a British writer, launched the Everyday Sexism Project. She created a website where people could share experiences of sexism. She hoped for 100 stories. By April 2015, the site had logged 100,000 entries. Branches opened in 25 countries.

On 16 December 2012 Jyoti Singh, a 23-year-old physiotherapy student, boarded a private bus in Delhi. The bus occupants gang-raped her. She died from her injuries on 29 December. Protests erupted at India Gate in New Delhi. The Indian government formed the Justice J.S. Verma Committee. Parliament passed the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 2013.

On 11 May 2015 the body of Chiara Páez, a 14-year-old girl from Rufino, Argentina, was found buried. She had been pregnant. Her boyfriend, 16, confessed. Journalist Marcela Ojeda tweeted. Within days, activists organized a mass protest for 3 June 2015 under the hashtag NiUnaMenos—Not One Less. Over 200,000 people gathered in Buenos Aires.

On 21 January 2017, the day after Donald Trump inauguration, an estimated 500,000 people gathered in Washington, D.C., for the Women March. Millions more marched in over 600 sister events worldwide. It was, at the time, the largest single-day protest in U.S. history.

On 5 October 2017 Jodi Kantor and Megan Twohey published an investigation in the New York Times: Harvey Weinstein had sexually harassed and assaulted women for decades. On 10 October Ronan Farrow published a second investigation in The New Yorker. On 15 October actress Alyssa Milano tweeted. Within 24 hours, the phrase me too appeared in 12 million posts. Milano had not known that Tarana Burke had been using the phrase since 2006. Black women on Twitter credited Burke. The hashtag MeToo became a global cascade.

sections.title: Ni Una Menos was Argentine; Delhi was Indian; none were American exports

blocks.text: Ni Una Menos in Argentina on 3 June 2015 is not an Argentine branch of an American franchise. It is a response to Argentine femicide, after the murder of an Argentine girl. The hashtag NiUnaMenos went viral in Argentina two years before MeToo went global. The movement had a name, a date, and demands before the Weinstein reporting.

The December 2012 Delhi case is an Indian fact. Jyoti Singh was an Indian student. The protests were at India Gate. The Criminal Law Amendment Act, 2013 is an Indian statute. The protests forced legal reform. This was not waiting for a cue from New York or Los Angeles.

sections.title: What a hashtag does not do

blocks.text: By 2026 the fourth-wave label is a classroom heading. The cascade has receded. Some of what it left behind: Weinstein in prison. Time's Up Legal Defense Fund still operating. Tarana Burke Me Too movement continuing as it always was: community-based, survivor-centered, not a hashtag. The Everyday Sexism Project still collecting stories.

What the hashtag did: it made the private public at a scale and speed that was new. The pattern was undeniable. It changed what could be said in workplaces. It did not end rape or harassment. It did not close the gender wage gap. Visibility is not the same as power. A cascade is not a revolution. Sometimes it becomes one. Sometimes it is just a flood that recedes.
When a cascade makes a pattern visible, who decides what counts as part of the pattern, and whose work gets remembered after the hashtag stops trending?
